This teaching page demonstrates why Quarto is valuable for a research group: narrative, executable Python, figures, computed tables, citations, and source code stay together.

::: {.callout-warning} ## Synthetic teaching data This is a deterministic classroom example—not a research benchmark and not field data. It illustrates the publishing workflow, not the performance of SeisReconNO. ::: ## Experiment We create a small synthetic seismic gather, remove a band of traces, and reconstruct the missing values with linear interpolation. A real research page could replace this toy method with a reviewed workflow related to neural-operator reconstruction [@traversa2026seisreconno]. ## Visual check ::: {#cell-fig-seismic-reconstruction .cell fig-height='4.2' fig-width='11' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 4.2), sharey=True) panels = [observed, damaged, reconstructed] titles = ["Synthetic observation", "Missing traces", "Interpolated baseline"] limit = np.nanpercentile(np.abs(observed), 99) for ax, panel, title in zip(axes, panels, titles): ax.imshow(panel, cmap="seismic", aspect="auto", vmin=-limit, vmax=limit, extent=[0, traces - 1, time[-1], time[0]]) ax.set_title(title) ax.set_xlabel("Trace") axes[0].set_ylabel("Time (s)") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Synthetic seismic gather before removal, with a missing trace band, and after simple interpolation.](python_files/figure-html/fig-seismic-reconstruction-output-1.png){#fig-seismic-reconstruction width=1047 height=394 fig-alt='Three seismic heatmaps showing complete data, a white central gap, and an interpolated reconstruction'} ::: ::: @fig-seismic-reconstruction is generated during rendering. Readers can expand the folded code, while the prose stays focused on interpretation. ## Computed quality summary ::: {#tbl-reconstruction-quality .cell tbl-cap='Error metrics inside the held-out trace band.' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} truth = observed[:, gap] estimate = reconstructed[:, gap] rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((truth - estimate) ** 2))) mae = float(np.mean(np.abs(truth - estimate))) signal_rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(truth**2))) metrics = pd.DataFrame({ "Metric": ["RMSE", "MAE", "Normalized RMSE"], "Value": [rmse, mae, rmse / signal_rms], }) metrics.style.format({"Value": "{:.3f}"}).hide(axis="index") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

RMSE 0.117

``` ::: ::: The values in @tbl-reconstruction-quality are computed from the same arrays shown in the figure, so a student cannot accidentally update one without the other. ## What students can test {.tabset} ### Analysis - Change the gap width or noise level. - Replace interpolation with another baseline. - Add an uncertainty or spectral-quality metric. ### Communication - Improve the figure caption and alternative text. - Explain where a simple baseline fails. - Add a source to `publications.bib` and cite it with `[@key]`. ### Reproducibility - Render locally and inspect `_freeze/`. - Confirm that the random seed keeps outputs stable. - Review the code and output together in a pull request. ## References ::: {#refs} :::
